To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

male veterans of prior conflicts have a suicide risk that is 1) higher than that of nonveterans, 2) higher than that found in prior research, 3) not statistically significantly different from that of nonveters, 4) not significantly different from the suicide risk of male veterans of the post-9/11 conflicts, and 5) higher than that reported in the Kaplan study.

male veterans of the pre-OIF/OEF conflicts have an age- adjusted suicide risk that is 1.3 (95% CI = 0.8–2.0) times greater than that of male nonveteran controls, and this risk is not significantly greater than that of nonveteran men after adjusting for sociodemographic factors, mental health disorders, and health behaviors.

the suicide risk among male OIF/OEF veterans is 2.3 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.3–4.2) times that among male nonveters, and the suicide risk among veterans of prior conflicts is 1.2 (95% CI: 1.0–1.5) times that among nonveterans.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the risk of suicide among male veterans who served during the Vietnam War and prior conflicts (hereafter referred to as “Vietnam-era veterans”); the research of Kaplan et al.7 is concerned with suicide risk among male OIF/OEF veterans.
a population that has been the focus of considerable research and policy attention.
the question of whether veterans are at higher risk of suicide than nonveterans and whether that risk varies by era.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of suicide among male OIF/OEF-era veterans is unknown and that the risk among male prior-era veterans is modestly higher than risk among nonveterans.
the risk of suicide among male veterans of prior conflicts is higher than that of nonveterans, but that the difference is not statistically significant and the magnitude of the difference is modest.
male veterans of the conflicts prior to OIF/OEF have a modestly higher, but not significantly different, age- and race- adjusted suicide risk compared with male nonveteran civilians.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our findings are consistent with those of other military cohort studies, but not with those of Kaplan et al.7

our findings are consistent with a small, but not significant, increase in suicide risk for male veterans of prior conflicts compared with male nonveteran controls, but we cannot rule out a modest increase in risk.
the suicide risk for male veterans of conflicts before OIF/OEF is not significantly higher than that of male nonveteran civilians.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the data used to date are not sufficient to answer pressing questions regarding suicide risk among veterans.
, despite the fact that suicide risk is elevated among male veterans of conflicts before OIF/OEF, this is not the case for male veterans of OIF/OEF.

the risk of suicide among veterans of prior conflicts remains a pressing public health problem, and that the current debate about the relative risk of suicide among OIF/OEF veterans versus male nonveteran peers is a distraction from the more important question of whether we can identify and intervene with the small subset of male veterans who are most at risk of suicide.
